title: Dil Chahta Hai Turns 25 in August. The Film That Taught the Diaspora How to Be Young Has Aged Better Than Any of Us.
excerpt: Saif Ali Khan looks back on the 105-day Goa shoot where the cast partied between takes — and a 26-year-old Farhan Akhtar quietly rewrote what Hindi cinema could be.
body:
There is a generation of NRIs who can tell you exactly where they were the first time they watched the three friends drive down to Goa in a borrowed car, the wind in their hair, *Kaisi Hai Yeh Rut* playing over the open road. For a lot of us, it was a cramped living room in New Jersey or Slough or Mississauga, a pirated VCD, a homesickness we didn't have words for yet. **Dil Chahta Hai** didn't just entertain us. It showed us a version of being Indian and being young that finally looked like the lives we were actually living — and it turns 25 this August.

<youtube></youtube>

The anniversary has sent the cast into a reflective mood, and the memories pouring out are as golden as the film itself. **Saif Ali Khan**, who played the lovably hopeless romantic Sameer, sat down with Variety India this week and the nostalgia practically dripped off him.

> "It was insane. I think it was the most fun because it was Goa, and we were very young." — Saif Ali Khan

He wasn't exaggerating. By his account, the shoot was less a job and more an extended holiday that happened to produce one of the most important films in Hindi cinema. "We shot on the beach and we partied as well," Saif recalled. "I remember we tried almost every restaurant in Goa. And because we were all so young, we had the energy to eat, drink, party and then come back for a shoot." You can feel it on screen — that loose, sun-drunk ease that no amount of craft can fake. The film looks like a group of friends having the time of their lives, because that is precisely what it was.

What makes the story irresistible, though, is the figure at the centre of all that chaos: a 26-year-old first-time director named **Farhan Akhtar**, son of a famous lyricist, with no proof yet that he could do this at all. Saif's verdict, a quarter-century later, is unequivocal.

> "We were laughing most of the time because Farhan wore it all very lightly. It was like he was born to direct, with the ease with which he was on a set. There was no tension, really." — Saif Ali Khan

That ease was deceptive. Behind the breeziness was a precision that stunned a notoriously chaotic industry. "I think it was the first time we had seen such efficient ADs," Saif said of the assistant directors. The crew had estimated a 105-day shoot after reading the script — and they wrapped on the 105th day. In a Bollywood that routinely ran months over schedule, that kind of discipline was almost radical. "We were just told to know our lines," Saif remembered. "No figuring it out once you get there. Just learn your lines and then the rest was great fun."

Released in 2001, **Dil Chahta Hai** arrived like a cultural reset. It gave us **Aamir Khan** as the commitment-phobic Akash with that now-mythologised goatee and spiky hair, **Akshaye Khanna** as the wounded, painterly Siddharth in the performance of his career, and Saif as the heart and sunshine of the whole thing. The **Shankar-Ehsaan-Loy** soundtrack became the sound of an entire era. The Goa road trip became a rite of passage. And the film's confident, urban, English-peppered sensibility told a liberalising India — and its children scattered across the West — that their lives were worthy of the big screen.

For the diaspora, the resonance ran even deeper. Here were characters who code-switched the way we did, who loved and sulked and grew up the way we were trying to. It is, quietly, one of the most rewatched Hindi films in NRI households on the planet, and it remains widely available — currently streaming on **Netflix** in most international markets, where a new generation of diaspora kids keep discovering it.

Twenty-five years on, the men who made it have scattered into very different careers — Saif into stardom and producing, Aamir into his cerebral blockbuster phase, Akshaye into a beloved character-actor renaissance, Farhan into directing, acting, and singing all at once. But for one impossibly young summer in Goa, they made something none of them have quite topped since. The rest of us just had the good fortune to grow up alongside it.
